A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we combine a micro-fluidics-based electric field chip with a nanoscale resolution imaging system to study the effects of EFs on cancer cells.

the filopodium growth of cancer cells is asymmetric under external dcEFs, and the biased filopodium growth is associated with the re-distribution of epidermal growth factors receptors (EGFRs) on the cell membrane.
cancer-cell filopaoida are sensitive to the external EF, and the asymmetric filopodium growth may be a novel biomarker for the diagnosis and treatment of cancers.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the MEC chip can be used to study the effects of endogenous EFs on cell behaviors in the microenvironment, and SINAP can be used to quantitatively measure the changes in cell filopodia in the presence of dcEF.
the growth of filopodium is asymmetrically biased under the dcEF stimulation and the growth rate of filopodium increases with the increase of EF intensity.
the filopodia growth and the EGF-receptor redistribution can be used as a quantitative index to evaluate the effect of EFs on cancer-cell behaviors.
